fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest change is that I started out thinking it would be hard, and it turned out to be almost embarrassingly easy.

When we began that project, my mental model was that the frontier models were converging. They train on roughly the same internet, they go through similar instruction tuning and preference optimization, and they're all being pushed toward the same notion of a helpful answer. So I expected that if you took a response from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, and asked a classifier to tell you which one wrote it, you'd land somewhere a bit above chance. Instead we got into the high nineties. Five-way classification, around ninety-seven percent. That number made me rethink what "convergence" actually means. The models may agree on content, but they have very distinct ways of saying things.

The second shift was about where the signal lives. My first guess was that it's mostly formatting, so markdown habits, bullet points, how often a model uses a heading. That's part of it, and you can see it just by eye. But when we stripped formatting, or rewrote the text, or translated it, the accuracy dropped but stayed far above chance. So the fingerprint is also in word choice, in phrasing, in how the model opens and closes an answer. These are things a human reader doesn't consciously notice, but they're very stable across prompts. It's a bit like handwriting. Each model has one, and it survives a lot of transformations.

The third change is that I now see this less as a detection problem and more as a measurement tool. If outputs carry a signature, then any dataset built from synthetic data carries that signature too. You can ask which model a given corpus was distilled from, or whether a new model was trained heavily on another model's outputs, just by looking at what it produces. That's a lineage question, and I think it will matter more and more as the field leans on synthetic data.

So the short version: I went in expecting the models to be interchangeable and the problem to be hard, and I came out thinking the models are quite individual, and that their individuality is something we can actually use.

r001.rationale: The response says stylistic signals can be seen by eye and are detectable by classifiers, but it does not clearly state that non-experts can infer which model generated a text.

r002.rationale: The response attributes differences to distinct training, tuning, and stylistic patterns, not to differing strategies for maximizing user engagement.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when we started I expected it to be a much harder problem than it turned out to be. These models are trained on roughly the same internet data, with similar architectures and similar recipes, and they're all tuned to sound like a helpful, polite assistant. So my prior was that their outputs would be close to interchangeable. Maybe you could tell them apart with a lot of effort, but not reliably.

That prior was quite wrong. The idea actually came from our earlier work on dataset bias in vision. There we found that a neural network can tell which of several large, supposedly generic image datasets an image came from, with surprisingly high accuracy. So we asked the same question for language models. If you take responses from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek and so on, can a classifier tell who wrote what? With a fairly standard setup, just fine-tuning a text embedding model, we got something like ninety-plus percent accuracy across five models. That was a real surprise to me.

What changed my thinking more was digging into where that signal comes from. Part of it is what you'd expect: certain favorite words and phrases, and formatting habits like how much markdown, how many bullet points, how the headers look. But then we had another model rewrite or translate the responses, and the accuracy stayed high. Even after summarizing, which strips out most of the style, you were still well above chance. So it isn't only surface tics. There's something in what the model chooses to say, what it emphasizes, and how it structures an answer.

So now I see it less as a forensic trick and more as a window into how these models are made. Each one carries a fingerprint from its particular data mixture, its post-training, and the preferences of the people who trained it. That has practical consequences. If you distill or train on another model's outputs, you inherit its idiosyncrasies, and that's detectable. It also made me more skeptical of the idea that all these models are converging to the same thing. They may be converging in capability, but they still have quite distinct personalities.

fable-5.text:
Thanks, Ravid — it's great to be here. So the biggest shift for me was going from thinking of this as a hard forensics problem to realizing it's almost embarrassingly easy. When we started that project, my intuition was that these models would be hard to tell apart. They're trained on largely overlapping internet data, many of them are tuned to sound like the same kind of helpful assistant, and if you just read their outputs side by side, they feel pretty interchangeable. I expected a classifier trained to guess which model wrote a given response would do a bit better than chance, maybe.

Instead, we found you can identify the source model with something like 97 percent accuracy on responses from the major chat models. Simply embed the text, train a classifier, and it just works. That really changed how I think about model outputs — every model has these idiosyncrasies, a kind of fingerprint, baked in at multiple levels.

The second update was about how deep those fingerprints go. My first guess was that the signal was mostly superficial — formatting habits, markdown usage, favorite opening phrases like "Certainly!" And some of it is. But when we tried to wash the signal out — paraphrasing the responses with another model, translating them, even summarizing them — the classifier still worked far above chance. So the identity of the model isn't just carried in surface style; it's in word choice distributions, in how the model organizes and structures an answer, in something closer to its semantic habits. That was surprising to me and honestly a little humbling, because it means these models are less "generic compressions of the internet" and more distinct characters than I'd assumed.

And the third shift is about why this matters. I originally thought of it as a curiosity, or maybe a tool for attribution — which model wrote this text. Now I think the more important implication is for training itself. So much of the field now trains on synthetic data, and if every model leaves a persistent fingerprint that survives rewriting, then when you train on another model's outputs, you're inheriting its idiosyncrasies. You can see lineage — which models were distilled from which — just by looking at outputs. So identification stopped being a detection question for me and became a lens on how model behaviors propagate through the whole ecosystem.

r001.rationale: The response describes a trained classifier identifying source models with high accuracy, but does not state that non-experts can infer which model generated a text.

r002.rationale: The response attributes output differences to persistent model fingerprints and training lineage, not to differing strategies for maximizing user engagement.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, it changed a lot, and mostly in the direction of "this is much easier than it should be."

When we started, my mental model was that the big models had converged. They're trained on overlapping web data, they're RLHF'd toward the same notion of helpfulness, and when you read two answers side by side they feel interchangeable. So I expected we'd need something clever — maybe long outputs, maybe careful statistical tests — to tell them apart.

Instead, you train a fairly ordinary text classifier on a few thousand responses and it separates the major chat models at well over ninety percent. Not from anything exotic. A lot of the signal is in things you'd dismiss as cosmetic: how the model formats a list, whether it bolds the lead-in to a bullet, which hedging phrases it reaches for, the marker words it likes. Each model has a dialect, and the dialect is loud.

The part that genuinely shifted my thinking was how stubborn it is. We paraphrased the outputs, we translated them into another language and back, we reduced them to summaries — and the classifier still works, degraded but well above chance. So it isn't only surface styling. There's something in the distribution underneath that survives being rewritten.

What that means practically is that model outputs carry a fingerprint, and fingerprints propagate. If you fine-tune on synthetic data from some model, your model inherits that signature. So in a world where everyone is training on everyone else's generations, identity is traceable in a way I didn't anticipate — which is useful for provenance, and somewhat uncomfortable if you were hoping your data pipeline was private.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Honestly, my view has moved from "this is surprising" to "this is almost inevitable." When we first ran the experiment, I expected distinguishing ChatGPT from Claude, Gemini, or DeepSeek to be hard. These models are trained to produce fluent, helpful, human-like text, and in a single response they can look very similar. But a fairly simple classifier could tell them apart with high accuracy, and that surprised me.

What I understand better now is where the signal comes from. It isn't mainly deep semantics. A lot of it sits in surface patterns: which words a model likes to start with, how it formats things, how it uses markdown and lists, and its favorite phrases. Even when we rewrote responses or shuffled them so the content was preserved but the style changed, the model-specific signal didn't disappear. That tells me these fingerprints are baked in by the training data and especially by post-training choices. Different companies make different decisions about what a good response looks like, and those decisions leave a trace in the output distribution.

The bigger shift for me is that I no longer see this as just a classification curiosity. It matters for synthetic data. If you train a new model on another model's outputs, you can inherit its quirks and biases without noticing, and those can compound across generations. It also changes how I think about "diversity" among models. We have many models with different names, but they may be less different than we assume, or they may differ in narrow, systematic ways that we haven't measured well.

I'm also more cautious about what we can conclude. Being able to identify a model doesn't mean we understand why the differences exist or whether they matter for capability. I think of it as a useful diagnostic, a way to see what a training pipeline did to a model, but not a complete explanation.

haiku-5.5.text: I think I started out treating it as a fairly clean detection problem. Given some text, can you tell which model wrote it? The answer often seemed to be yes, sometimes with surprising accuracy. The longer I looked at those results, the less I believed the signal was a stable fingerprint. What the classifier picks up is probably a mix of training data, post-training style, and the particular habits each alignment process instills, and those habits shift across checkpoints and settings. So I'm less inclined to read identification accuracy as evidence of a unique signature. I'm more interested in what the signal is actually tracking, and whether it survives paraphrasing, different sampling choices, or fine-tuning. Getting the label right is only part of the question.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more cautious about what it means to identify a model from its output. You can notice a particular style or a tendency to use certain phrases, but that’s different from having reliable evidence that an answer came from a particular model. The prompt can change those things, and different models can produce very similar answers.

So I would frame it more as a statistical question: given these outputs, how much evidence do we have for one model versus another? And how much does that conclusion depend on which models we’re considering? Picking among a few known candidates is a much narrower problem than identifying an arbitrary model in the wild. I still think the question is interesting, but I’m less comfortable treating a recognizable writing style as a definitive fingerprint.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more cautious about what it means to identify a model. It’s tempting to imagine that every model has a fingerprint, and you can look at an answer and say, “Okay, this came from that model.” But the output also depends on the prompt, the sampling settings, and whatever instructions are wrapped around the model.

So I would now frame the question more narrowly: among a particular set of candidate models, under particular conditions, how much evidence do the outputs give you? You might distinguish them quite well in that setting, but that doesn’t automatically tell you how well the method works after fine-tuning or when a new model appears.

I still think it’s an interesting problem. I’m just more interested now in understanding which signals are stable and how much confidence they justify. Recognizing a familiar style is one thing; establishing where an output came from requires stronger evidence.
